newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Landmine victims soar in Afghan capital.
newsitem.headline: Landmine victims soar in Afghan capital.

text.p: The number of people killed or injured by landmines in Kabul soared in October, and most of the victims were children, an international aid group said on Monday.

Save the Children (USA) said in a statement that 37 percent of the deaths and injuries caused by landmines and unexploded bombs in Kabul over the past six months had occurred in October, after the purist Islamic Taleban took the Afghan capital.

It cited one case in which a farmer's daughters, aged six and seven, went to visit him in a field on the outskirts of the city. "As they spread a cloth on the ground and prepared to sit down, a landmine exploded underneath," it said.
The aid group said one daughter was killed instantly and the other died in hospital.
It said 66 of the 85 people killed or injured in October were children and that the real numbers were probably higher because it was able to count only the victims brought to Kabul's main hospitals.
The total did not include those killed outright. They are buried swiftly under Islamic custom and are not taken to hospital. Nor did the total include those taken to clinics.
The aid group did not give figures for the whole of Afghanistan, where millions of mines have been laid in 17 years of conflict, first against Soviet occupation and then in a civil war.
But it attributed the rise in Kabul last month partly to the closure of most schools by the Taleban, who imposed Islam's stern Sharia law on the city when they took over on September 27.
They barred girls from going to school, a policy that would be revised when Afghanistan is at peace, the Taleban say, and only a few boys schools have re-opened.
"Children are spending more time wandering about and playing outside, thereby increasing their chances of being injured," the aid group said.
It said the relative peace that came to Kabul when the Taleban took over after four years of factional fighting that left swathes of the city in ruins had also contributed to the higher total.
"Residents have begun moving around in areas that were previously inaccessible to them -- these areas tend to be strewn with mines and unexploded ordnance," it said.
"The onset of winter has meant that many more people, children in particular, are out foraging for firewood, an extremely dangerous activity in this mine-infested city," it added.
The group cited a 1995 survey as saying 22 sq km (8.5 sq m) of Kabul were mined, half in residential areas.
Several Western aid groups are working in Afghanistan to help clear mines. They say the situation has improved since 1995 and that about 90 percent of the city has been cleared.
But they confess it is a long, slow job and that new fighting inevitably means more mines are laid.
The Taleban is currently fighting a northern alliance over a band of hills 25-30 km (15-20 miles) north of the capital.
The loss of the hills would mean Kabul, once again, would be threatened.
